questions.question: Explain the nature and interdisciplinary character of Organizational Behaviour. / [CO1]
questions.solution_html:
• Explain the nature and interdisciplinary character of Organizational Behaviour. .(U /CO1)
  • Organizational Behaviour (OB) is the study of how people act, think, and feel inside
  • workplace organizations. Its nature is practical and evidence-based—it helps managers
  • understand human behavior to solve real workplace problems, improve employee
  • performance, and increase job satisfaction. OB looks at behavior at three levels: Individual
  • (personality, learning), Group (teamwork, leadership), and Organization (culture, structure).
  • It is also flexible (contingent), meaning there is no single "best way" to manage people; the
  • right approach depends on the situation. OB has an interdisciplinary character because it
  • borrows ideas from several social sciences like Psychology: Gives insights into individual
  • personality, perception, learning, and motivation.Sociology: Helps explain group behavior,
  • team dynamics, organizational structure, and culture.Social Psychology: Explains
  • communication, attitude changes, and decision-making in teams.Anthropology: Helps us
  • understand cross-cultural differences and global work environments.Political Science:
  • Explains workplace power, office politics, and conflict resolution.
  • (definition 1mark,nature 2 and interdisciplinary 2 mark)

questions.question: Explain the major factors that contribute to individual differences in personality. / [CO2]
questions.solution_html:
• Explain the major factors that contribute to individual differences in personality.
  • .(U /CO2)
  • Individual differences mean that every employee is unique in how they think, feel, and
  • behave at work. Personality is the stable set of characteristics that determines how a person
  • reacts to different situations. Personality is formed by two main forces: Nature (Heredity) and
  • Nurture (Environment).
  • Biological & Heredity Factors (Nature): Genes inherited from parents play a major role in
  • shaping physical traits, temperament, energy levels, and brain function. Research shows that
  • genetics account for about 50% of personality differences.
  • Environmental Factors (Nurture): A person's upbringing, family values, school education,
  • peer groups, and societal culture shape their habits and moral beliefs. For example, people
  • raised in individualist cultures value personal independence, while those in collectivist
  • cultures value group teamwork.
  • Situational & Learning Experiences: Life experiences, career changes, and continuous
  • learning help refine and stabilize a person's personality traits over time.
  • (intro 1 mark-any two factors two mark each)

questions.question: Explain decision by experts and Decision by averaging individual’s opinions as Group/Team Decision-making techniques. / [CO3]
questions.solution_html:
• Explain Decision by Experts and Decision by Averaging Individual's Opinions as
  • Group/Team Decision-making techniques. .(U /CO3)
  • (Intro 1 mark two mark each for each technique)
  • In team decision-making, when full group discussion is not possible or time is limited, teams
  • use these two non-discussion techniques:
  • Decision by Experts: The team hands over the entire decision to one member who has the
  • most technical knowledge or experience in that area.
  • It is fast and works very well for complex technical problems.
  • Disadvantages: Finding the true expert can be difficult, and if the wrong person is picked, a
  • poor decision is made. Other team members may also feel left out.
  • Decision by Averaging Individual's Opinions: The leader collects individual ratings, scores,
  • or votes from each member separately (through forms or messages) and calculates the
  • average score to make the final decision without a live group meeting.
  • It saves time, stops loud members from dominating, and gives everyone an equal say.
  • Disadvantages: There is no group debate to create new ideas, and expert opinions get the
  • exact same weight as beginner opinions

questions.question: Differentiate job rotation, job enlargement and job enrichment in terms of how each changes a job. / [CO3]
questions.solution_html:
• Differentiate job rotation, job enlargement, and job enrichment in terms of how each
  • changes a job.(U /CO2)
  • Job design defines how work tasks are structured, and organizations use job rotation, job
  • enlargement, and job enrichment to reduce employee boredom and boost motivation. Job
  • rotation changes a job by horizontally moving an employee from one simple task to another
  • at set times (such as moving a fast-food worker from cooking fries to operating the cash
  • register) without changing task difficulty or worker authority, which reduces physical fatigue
  • and creates a multi-skilled workforce. Job enlargement expands the horizontal scope of a
  • job by adding more tasks of the same skill level to a worker's daily routine (such as asking a
  • typist to also answer phones and greet visitors), which increases task variety and breaks
  • single-task monotony but gives the worker no extra decision-making power. In contrast, job
  • enrichment expands the vertical depth of a job by giving the employee higher responsibility,
  • freedom, and decision-making control (such as allowing a factory worker to plan their own
  • schedule, assemble the entire product, inspect quality, and speak with suppliers), which
  • directly satisfies growth needs, builds self-confidence, and creates high internal work
  • motivation and job satisfaction.

questions.question: Explain how learning takes place through Online Training. / [CO2]
questions.solution_html:
• Explain how learning takes place through Online Training. (K/CO2)
  • Online training (or E-Learning) is a digital instruction system where trainers and trainees are
  • physically separated, and lessons are delivered using computers, smartphones, videos, and
  • Learning Management Systems. Learning happens online through four simple step-by-step
  • processes: first, complex courses are broken into short lessons followed by quick quizzes,
  • where receiving immediate digital feedback acts as positive reinforcement to help students
  • quickly correct mistakes and lock in knowledge; second, by combining written text with
  • audio, diagrams, and videos, online modules engage both logical and visual brain processing,
  • making difficult concepts easier to understand; third, trainees learn through observation by
  • watching video demonstrations of experts performing skills, which builds self-efficacy and
  • confidence before attempting the task on the job; and finally, learners go through a complete
  • experiential cycle by watching scenario videos, participating in online discussion forums,
  • reading digital materials, and testing their skills in interactive exercises, allowing them to
  • learn at their own comfortable pace.
  • (Students are either free to write similar to scheme or using examples )

questions.question: Explain Delphi technique as a decision making generating alternative technique. / [CO3] [5x4 = 20]
questions.solution_html:
• Explain Delphi Technique as a decision-making generating alternative technique. .(U
  • /CO3)
  • The Delphi Technique is a structured group decision-making method used to solve complex
  • problems by gathering expert opinions through sequential questionnaires, with the unique
  • feature that the experts never meet face-to-face. It was specifically created to overcome
  • common meeting problems—such as dominant bosses controlling the room, loud
  • personalities, and the fear of disagreeing with senior staff (groupthink)—by keeping every
  • participant's answers completely anonymous throughout the process. The method begins
  • when a central leader selects a panel of experts and sends them a first questionnaire to collect
  • initial ideas anonymously; the leader collects and summarizes these responses into a report,
  • then sends a second questionnaire where experts rate and score all the generated alternatives;
  • through two to three iterative rounds of scoring and feedback, experts adjust their ratings
  • based on group averages until a common agreement (consensus) is reached, producing a
  • high-quality, expert-driven decision without incurring travel costs or suffering from peer
  • pressure.
  • (5x4=20)

questions.question: Define social ,emotional and appreciative intelligence and explain its significance for effective leadership. / [CO2]
questions.solution_html:
• Define social, emotional, and appreciative intelligence and explain its significance for
  • effective leadership.(U/Co2)
  • (Each factor 3 marks each and 1 mark for intro and conclu)
  • Social, emotional, and appreciative intelligence represent three critical interpersonal
  • capabilities that drive effective leadership beyond traditional intellectual ability (IQ). Social
  • intelligence is the ability to perceive, interpret, and understand social dynamics accurately,
  • allowing leaders to adapt their behavior across diverse interpersonal contexts and navigate
  • workplace politics smoothly. Emotional intelligence (EI), popularized by Daniel Goleman
  • and rooted in Salovey and Mayer's framework, is the capacity to monitor, understand, and
  • regulate one's own emotions and those of others through five core dimensions: self-
  • awareness, self-regulation, internal motivation, empathy, and social skills. Appreciative
  • intelligence, developed by Thatchenkery and Metzker, is the ability to perceive the positive,
  • inherent generative potential within a present situation or person, comprising three key
  • components: reframing tasks with purpose, appreciating positive aspects, and seeing how a
  • successful future unfolds from present actions. Together, these three intelligences are vital for
  • effective leadership because they enable managers to handle organizational change and
  • employee anxiety during crises, build trust across multicultural teams, resolve interpersonal
  • conflicts, and create positive self-fulfilling prophecies that inspire innovation and peak
  • performance.

questions.question: Explain Herzberg’s Two-Factor Theory of Motivation. How its contribution to work motivation apply in work setting / [CO3]
questions.solution_html:
• Explain Herzberg's Two-Factor Theory of Motivation. How does its contribution to work
  • motivation apply in a work setting? (A/Co3)
  • (Explaining the theory fetches 5 marks and application 5 marks)
  • Frederick Herzberg's Two-Factor (or Motivator-Hygiene) Theory asserts that job satisfaction
  • and job dissatisfaction are driven by two entirely separate sets of workplace factors rather
  • than existing on a single continuous scale. Hygiene factors pertain to the job context or
  • working environment—such as company policies, technical supervision, physical working
  • conditions, base salary, job security, and interpersonal relationships—and serve a preventive
  • role; improving them eliminates employee dissatisfaction and brings morale to a neutral
  • baseline, but does not actively inspire superior performance. In contrast, motivators relate
  • directly to job content and the nature of the work itself—including achievement, recognition,
  • challenging assignments, increased responsibility, advancement, and personal growth—
  • which satisfy higher-level growth needs and generate genuine internal motivation and job
  • satisfaction. In a practical work setting, managers must apply this theory through a two-step
  • approach: first, they must manage hygiene factors by providing fair compensation, safe
  • working environments, and equitable policies to remove grievances and prevent turnover;
  • second, once baseline hygiene is established, they must implement vertical job enrichment by
  • delegating decision-making autonomy, offering meaningful recognition, structuring complete
  • work modules, and providing clear career growth paths to drive long-term productivity and
  • engagement.

questions.question: Discuss the professional skills required by managers at different levels of the organizational hierarchy. / [CO1] [10x2 = 20]
questions.solution_html:
• Discuss the professional skills required by managers at different levels of the
  • organizational hierarchy. (U/Co1)
  • (Some students may write only Henry Mintzberg identified ten distinct roles that managers
  • perform, which are grouped into three primary categories: interpersonal, informational, and
  • decisional .)
  • Managerial effectiveness across an organizational hierarchy relies on a balanced combination
  • of four core professional skills identified are : technical skills (applying specialized methods,
  • tools, and procedures), interpersonal (human) skills (working effectively with people,
  • motivating teams, and resolving conflict), conceptual skills (viewing the organization as an
  • interconnected whole, analyzing complex environments, and engaging in strategic planning),
  • and communication skills (clearly conveying thoughts and actively listening, which
  • underpins all managerial interactions). The relative importance of these skills varies
  • significantly across the three main levels of the corporate hierarchy: first-line managers
  • (supervisors) require high technical skills to train operational employees, inspect work
  • quality, and solve daily technical problems, paired with strong interpersonal skills to handle
  • routine worker concerns; middle managers (department heads) serve as a crucial bridge
  • between executive vision and operational execution, relying heavily on interpersonal and
  • communication skills to coordinate cross-functional teams alongside moderate conceptual
  • skills to translate strategy into action; and top-level executives (CEOs) depend primarily on
  • high conceptual skills to navigate environmental uncertainty, make long-range strategic
  • choices, and shape organizational vision, while relying on staff experts for day-to-day
  • technical execution.
